passage: I'm Ayesha, and I sit behind Keerthana. When the science tests came back, she got 14 out of 20 and smiled. Then she turned and saw Chandni's paper: 20 out of 20, with a star. Keerthana's smile dropped. She folded her paper in half so no one could see and put her head on the desk. At break she didn't eat her idli. Then Ma'am said, "This was a hard test. The class average was only 9." Keerthana sat straight up and unfolded her paper. "Fourteen is five more than average!" she told me, grinning. I don't know exactly what she felt. But the paper said 14 the whole time.

qa.q: What was the class average?
qa.a: Only 9.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana fold her paper after seeing Chandni's mark?
qa.a: Next to Chandni's 20 with a star, her 14 suddenly felt bad, so she seemed embarrassed and didn't want anyone to see it.

qa.q: What could Keerthana ask herself next time before reacting to a friend's mark?
qa.a: She could ask what she understood and what she missed, judging her 14 by her own learning instead of by whoever sits nearby.

qa.q: How does Ayesha see Keerthana's change of mood?
qa.a: Ayesha notices the paper said 14 the whole time and only what Keerthana compared it with changed, though Ayesha can't be sure what Keerthana felt.

grounding: A classmate watches a girl feel miserable about a fair score beside a friend's top mark, then delighted on hearing the low class average.

passage:
Monday: Rashmi got 32 out of 50 in maths and felt fine. It was more than last time.
Tuesday: At lunch, Yash said he got 48. "Only two wrong!" Rashmi pushed her rice around. At home she told Amma she was "the worst at maths in the whole world" and wouldn't show her the paper.
Thursday: Sir wrote the class scores on the board, without names. Most were in the twenties. Rashmi counted. Hers was the fifth highest. She ran home, slapped the paper on the table and said, "Amma, I'm actually good!" Amma looked at the paper. It was the same 32 Rashmi had refused to show her on Tuesday.

qa.q: How many marks did Rashmi get in maths?
qa.a: 32 out of 50.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling on Tuesday when she called herself "the worst at maths"?
qa.a: She felt miserable and ashamed, because Yash's 48 made her own 32 look tiny.

qa.q: What could Amma say on Thursday to help Rashmi next time?
qa.a: She could point out gently that it's the same 32, and ask how it compares with Rashmi's own last test, so her feelings rest on her own progress, not only on others' marks.

qa.q: How might Yash feel if he knew his "Only two wrong!" upset Rashmi?
qa.a: Yash was just happy about his score and probably didn't mean to hurt anyone, so he might feel surprised or sorry. 😅

grounding: Across a week, a girl's feeling about the same maths score swings from content to miserable to delighted depending on whose marks she compares it with.

passage: Usha, sit here. You're sulking because your friend got more marks, na? Let me tell you about your Vishal Dadu at ten. In our village school near Gorakhpur, I got sixty in the half-yearly exam. I was so happy, running home to show my mother. On the way, my friend Bhola showed me his: ninety-five. Suddenly my sixty felt like a stone in my hand. I hid the paper under my mattress and didn't eat my dinner. Next day, Masterji announced that most of the class had got below forty. Forty! I pulled that paper out so fast. I was a king again. Same sixty, Usha. Only the thing I held it next to had changed.

qa.q: What did Bhola get in the exam?
qa.a: Ninety-five.

qa.q: Why did young Vishal hide the paper under his mattress?
qa.a: Next to Bhola's ninety-five, his sixty felt like a stone, so he felt ashamed and didn't want anyone to see it.

qa.q: What choice could young Vishal have made on the way home that might have saved his dinner?
qa.a: He could have held on to how pleased he was before Bhola showed his paper, or found out how the rest of the class did before deciding his sixty was bad.

qa.q: Why might Dadu be telling Usha this story now?
qa.a: Usha is sulking over a friend's higher marks, and Dadu wants to show, through his own boyhood, that the feeling depends on what the marks are compared with.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how, as a boy, the same exam score felt shameful beside a friend's mark and wonderful once he heard the class did worse.

passage: The school bus was stuck in a jam near the market, horns blaring, and Jagdish had forty minutes to stare at his English paper: 26 out of 40. He had been quite pleased when Ma'am handed it back. Then Preeti, beside him, showed hers: 38, with 'Excellent!' in green. Now his 26 looked terrible. His grandfather would ask about it at dinner. Jagdish folded the paper small and stuffed it in his bag. 'I'm hopeless,' he muttered. At the next stop, Preeti's mother climbed on, reading her phone. 'Ma'am has messaged the parents' group. The class average was only 21. Very hard paper, she says.' Jagdish sat up. He unfolded the paper. Twenty-six. Above average! By the time the bus reached his lane, he was grinning and practising how to tell Dadaji.

qa.q: What did Jagdish score in English?
qa.a: He scored 26 out of 40.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish mutter 'I'm hopeless'?
qa.a: Next to Preeti's 38 with 'Excellent!', his 26 suddenly felt terrible, and he worried about telling his grandfather.

qa.q: What could Jagdish ask himself next time he compares marks?
qa.a: He could ask what his mark means on its own, whether he improved or how hard the paper was, instead of judging it only against a friend's top score.

qa.q: How might Preeti have felt seeing Jagdish fold his paper away?
qa.a: Preeti might have felt awkward that showing that mark made a friend upset, without meaning to.

grounding: A boy's same mark feels terrible next to a friend's top score and wonderful once he hears the class average, showing the reference point changed the feeling.

passage: In the Pune colony's evening tuition class, Chaitanya got his maths practice test back: 55 out of 100. He shrugged. Not bad. Then Lalit, at the next desk, waved his paper. '92! Beat that!' Chaitanya's ears went hot. Suddenly 55 looked like a failure. He slid the paper under his notebook and didn't answer the next question Sir asked. Then Sir tapped the board. 'This was an olympiad-level test. Most of you are between 30 and 45. The average is 38.' Chaitanya looked at his paper again. 55. Seventeen above average! He pulled it out and smoothed it flat. On the walk home through the colony, he swung his bag and told the watchman, the vegetable seller and his mother, in that order.

qa.q: What was the class average on the practice test?
qa.a: The average was 38.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya's ears go hot when Lalit waved his paper?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, because next to Lalit's 92 his 55 suddenly looked like a failure.

qa.q: Which question could help Chaitanya judge his mark more steadily?
qa.a: He could ask how hard the test was and how he did compared with his own past, rather than only comparing with Lalit's top mark.

qa.q: How might Lalit see Chaitanya after the average was announced?
qa.a: Lalit might notice his friend cheer up and realise that both of them did well on a very hard test.

grounding: A boy feels miserable about his fair mark after a friend's top score, then delighted when he hears the low class average, though his mark never changed.
